Where should I start.  My background is in hacking, and Hacknet annoyed me.  I already know unix commands, I felt entitled enough at the start to scoff at the simulated terminal's shortcomings.  No top? No df/du? No ability to create directories even? Pfft.

But then I stopped and listened.  I remembered the kick-ass tunes in the best hacking films of yesteryear, particularly Hackers, and I stopped expecting realism and just tried to enjoy the game for the atmosphere.  And there were moments during my first play through where I actually, uncontrollably, smiled like a kid at christmas.  You see, the beauty in this  game is that thinking like a hacker gets you places, and it's rewarding to once more feel that, even if just for a short time.  I won't spoil the game for anybody, but there were 3 points during my playthrough where I felt ridiculously happy.  The rest of it was entertaining but would have been bland if not for a compelling story and surprisingly good characterisation, given the short nature of the game.  But that's also my greatest criticism.  I can forgive the subset of 'nix commands, the hokey visualisations that accompany your hacking tools and the ultra cheesy faux corporation names, but the real problem it the game leaves you wanting a hell of a lot more when it's over.  There is a multiplayer version in the pipe (see what I did there), but I wasn't able to find much on upcoming features other than the dev is currently working on ports for mac and linux, which is fine but doesn't interest me since I mostly game on windoze.  But I want more plots, more things to hack, more tools.  I want modding, I want more of that amazing retro-themed music (particularly that ONE track, again, no spoilers. If you've completed the game, you know the one).  I want that track to kick in more than once a play-through, when I'm doing something crazy important and urgent in the game.  

TL;DR? Ex-hacker got nostalgic playing indie hacking game, had feels, loved it enough to write a review. 
5/10 for replayability of the game as it is currently.
10/10 for some obvious and not-so-obvious references to Hackers and other hacking esotera.

Overall, 10/10 if, and when, RPG-like elements like upgrading equipment, infinite procedural mission/story generation, and bouncing connections/more advanced tracing dynamics are introduced.  I know, I'm demanding.
For now? 8/10 for the most fun 6 hours of a game I've had since Portal 2.

Summary: Hacknet is a fantastic hacker game; adding a terminal element sets it apart from other games in the genre such as Uplink: Hacker Elite. While in between storyline hacks the game leaves players feeling like their hacks have little reward or purpose, the stunning gameplay, visuals, and story make this game a must buy if you enjoy computers and being stressed out of your mind.

Hacking games such as this are always a thrill, at least in my experience. Nothing gets your heart racing more than a big red countdown as your fingers slip trying to type in a password. Hacknet is a great example of this genre.

Games such as Uplink: Hacker Elite have the player take part in "Hollywood hacking", using things like password crackers and dragging bypassers over network elements. While Hacknet it far from realistic hacking, the addition of the terminal makes the game so much better. While clicking and dragging can take time, it is far more stressful to type commands under pressure than it is to click them. This is one of Hacknet's biggest strengths, and players even have the ability to completely remove the user interface and play the game strictly through the terminal.

However, as I play Hacknet, there are periods of time where I'm not quite sure what I'm trying to acheive. I accept a contract, complete a hack, and at the end receive an email with a rank out of 100. This is where I think Uplink has the advantage; as you completed jobs you were paid money in order to upgrade you computer hardware and software. In Hacknet, the only time I really feel purposeful in my hacking in when I'm working on a hack relating to the story.

On top of great gameplay, the visuals of Hacknet are astounding. Just before writing this review I had a trace complete on me during a hack, and was greeting with the scariest red screen I've ever seen. The following sequence of trying to fix my mistake (I won't spoil anything!) was absolutely the most stressful thing I've experienced in a game.

Hacknet also has a great story (at least so far!), and I'm having trouble tearing myself away from the screen. All in all this game is a definite buy if you're into computers and having a heartrate of over 150.

Hacknet is quite hard to describe. Technically, it's a game where you, err, Hack networks. Essentially, the game hands you a UNIX command line, then gives you a bunch of IPs leading to servers filled with all kinds of side missions and challenges. You take on each job by following a carefully assorted set of IPs which usually lead you down a giant rabbit hole to a hidden server with extreme security that contains the target file that you have to steal, delete or edit.

The underlying atmosphere of Hacknet is perfect. Following long, hidden trails of IPs that lead to corporate secrets feels so right. Hacknet is just a game of "Fuck with other people's stuff", but it's so damn satisfying. Altering web servers to change their text, editing online savegames, reading people's emails, finding account credentials and editing medical records has never been so fun (implying I did that kind of stuff before I played Hacknet).

The story isn't really anything special, but it's still there and it's interesting. The game begins, then ignores the story until the end, instead sending you off on an epic quest to deface "Nortron Security's" website. Suddenly you're contacted at the end of the game, which leads you into a the final questline where you find out the secrets of the hacker named "Bit".

The puzzle-type gameplay is on the ball. The game leaves you to your own device and lets you work everything out for yourself. Honestly, I ended up looking up a good bit of it. Your job might be to accquire credentials for a company server, so you then set off, deciding where you're going to look, without the game's support. Will you try to find an employee's email? Or will you search for a company computer, then break into it and search for a text file that might contain a password? Maybe you'll even scan the company's network from there and find a hidden server protected by an unknown type of security?

And that just about sums up my relatively vague review...

I've been looking for new games, and nothing has really interested me until I looked at Hacknet again...
The concept of Hacknet is probably the best I've seen in a lot of recent games. The game has a steep learning curve, but when you overcome that, hacking into PCs and server is actually simpler than you think.

The only insight you get when you start up the game is a quick tutorial, teaching you the very bare-bones basics of the hacking. After that, you're on your own. YOU have to teach yourself how to utilize your tools to get the jobs done. You'll get very brief instructions whenever you acquire a new program, but other than that - you learn on the fly.

You accept contracts from various hacker groups (which you have to prove your abilities to enter), leading you all over the cybernet to complete them. There are tons of easter eggs and extra content, one of my favorites being the Shrine of the Polar Star. 

The feeling you get when you overcome an especially secure machine is great. It's also fun to come across something you couldn't crack before, but now you realize, "Hey, I can crack this no problem." 

Also, the OST is AMAZING. If you can, get the deluxe edition that includes the OST.
